title: Entrepreneurship and Startup Basics
tagline: From problem to pilot to pitch, with practice in every module
summary: Learn how to start a venture sensibly: find a real problem, talk to customers, test cheaply, design a business model, understand unit economics and cash, win customers, choose funding and pitch. Every module has a hands-on lab.

modules.title: Ideas and problems
modules.summary: Find real problems worth solving and describe them with evidence.
modules.outcome: You can tell problems from solutions, find problems through observation and write a problem statement with a customer, a cost and a size.
modules.intro: Most start-ups fail not because the product was bad, but because nobody needed it badly enough. The cure is to begin with a problem that real people have and are already trying to solve.

topics.title: What entrepreneurs do
topics.html:
Definition

Entrepreneurship. Creating value by turning an opportunity into an organisation, product or service, accepting uncertainty and risk in the hope of a reward for customers, the founders and often society.

Kinds of ventures
KindTypical aimExample
Small or lifestyle businessA good living and independenceA neighbourhood bakery
Scalable start-upRapid growth and large marketA software platform
Social enterpriseSolve a social problem with a sustainable modelAffordable clean-cooking stoves
IntrapreneurshipNew ventures inside a companyA new product team at a bank

There is no single type of founder. Successful founders include teenagers, retirees, scientists and shopkeepers. What they share is not a personality but a habit: they learn from real customers faster than their competitors.

Skills that can be learned

  1. Spotting problems
  2. Talking to customers
  3. Testing cheap experiments
  4. Counting money carefully
  5. Selling and persuading
  6. Working with others and handling setbacks
Watch out

Starting a business involves financial risk. Do not borrow or invest money you cannot afford to lose, and take proper advice on legal and tax matters.

Check what you just learned

1. What do successful founders share?
  • A particular age
  • A habit of learning from customers (correct)
  • A rich family
  • A degree

Learning speed matters.
keyPoints: Entrepreneurs create value by solving problems under uncertainty.
The key habit is learning quickly from customers.

topics.title: Finding problems worth solving
topics.html:
Where good problems hide

  • Your own frustrations: what annoys you repeatedly?
  • Work you or your family do: what is slow, costly or error-prone?
  • People who spend money or time on poor workarounds.
  • Changes in technology, law or habits that create new needs.
  • Places where products sold elsewhere are missing locally.
A problem is worth solving when
TestQuestion
FrequentHow often does it happen?
PainfulHow much does it cost in time, money or stress?
WidespreadHow many people have it?
Current spendAre people already paying or trying to fix it?
ReachableCan I find and talk to them?
Worked example

Observation

A student notices that a long queue at the college canteen means many classmates skip lunch.

  1. Frequent: every day.
  2. Painful: 30 minutes lost or a skipped meal.
  3. Widespread: thousands on campus.
  4. Already spending: 80 rupees a day on an average meal.
  5. Reachable: you are one of them.

Answer. A well-chosen problem passes most of the tests.

Tip

Write your idea as a problem first: 'People like X struggle to do Y because Z.' If you cannot, you do not yet understand the problem.

Check what you just learned

1. Which is a better start?
  • I want to build an app
  • A cool logo
  • People like X struggle with Y because Z (correct)
  • A name

Begin with the problem.
keyPoints: Look for frequent, painful, widespread problems people already pay to fix.
Write the problem before the product.

topics.title: Describing the problem with evidence
topics.html:
The four parts of a problem statement
PartContent
WhoThe specific customer
ProblemWhat goes wrong and why
SizeHow many people and how big is the cost?
TodayHow do they cope now and why is that not enough?

The 'today' part is the most overlooked. Your real competitor is not another start-up; it is whatever customers do now, even if that is doing nothing, using a spreadsheet or paying a relative. Understanding it tells you what you must beat.

How big is the problem?

Change the numbers to see the yearly money spent on the problem by the customers you could reach. This is a teaching estimate, not a real market study.

Adjust Customers you could reach, Times per year they face it, Rupees spent each time and see Yearly spend on the problem (rupees), If you won 5% of it change.

Common mistakes

  • Describing your solution instead of the problem.
  • Using a huge number such as 'a billion people' without narrowing.
  • Ignoring how people cope today.

Check what you just learned

1. The most overlooked part of a problem statement is:
  • The logo
  • The founder's name
  • The colour
  • How customers cope today (correct)

It is your real competition.

Key terms: flip and sort

Entrepreneur
Someone who creates a venture to meet a need
Problem statement
A description of who has what problem
Workaround
How customers cope without a good solution
Scalable
Able to grow without proportional cost
Social enterprise
A business with a social mission
keyPoints: Write who, problem, size and today.
Your real competition is current behaviour.

modules.title: Customers and validation
modules.summary: Talk to customers, test your riskiest assumptions and build the smallest thing that teaches you something.
modules.outcome: You can run customer interviews without leading questions, separate evidence from polite opinions and design a minimum viable test.
modules.intro: Validation means finding out cheaply whether people really want what you plan to build. It protects your savings, your time and your enthusiasm.

topics.title: Customer interviews
topics.html:
The goal of a customer interview is to learn about the customer's life, not to sell or to get compliments. People are polite and will praise your idea. Their past behaviour is far more reliable than their promises.

Good and bad questions
Bad (leading or hypothetical)Better (past behaviour)
Would you use an app that finds study rooms?Tell me about the last time you looked for a study room.
Do you like my idea?What do you do now when the library is full?
Would you pay 100 rupees?What have you paid for to solve this before?
Don't you think lunch is a problem?Walk me through your last lunch break.

Interview habits

  1. Talk to at least ten to twenty real customers, not friends.
  2. Ask open questions and then stay quiet.
  3. Ask 'why?' and 'tell me more'.
  4. Take notes and look for patterns.
  5. Never pitch during the interview.
  6. Thank them and ask who else you should talk to.
Tip

If every answer is 'yes, great idea', you probably asked the wrong questions.

Check what you just learned

1. A better interview question is:
  • Tell me about the last time you had this problem (correct)
  • Would you buy this?
  • Do you like my logo?
  • Isn't this great?

Past behaviour predicts.
keyPoints: Ask about the past, not the future; never pitch.
Talk to many real customers and look for patterns.

topics.title: Assumptions and evidence
topics.html:
Every business plan rests on assumptions: that customers have the problem, will pay, can be reached and that you can deliver at a profit. The riskiest assumptions are those that, if wrong, would kill the idea and about which you know least.

Strong and weak evidence
StrongWeak
Customers pay money or pre-orderFriends say it is a great idea
Customers give time or reputation (introduce you to others)Likes on social media
Repeat purchase'I might use it'
Signed agreement or depositA survey of 'maybe'
Watch out

Beware of fooling yourself. Founders tend to hear what they hope to hear. Decide in advance what result would make you change course.

Check what you just learned

1. Which is strong evidence of demand?
  • A friend's compliment
  • Twelve customers paying in advance (correct)
  • Likes
  • A survey of maybe

Money talks.
keyPoints: Test the riskiest assumption first with the cheapest experiment.
Money, time and repeat behaviour are strong evidence.

topics.title: Minimum viable tests
topics.html:
Definition

Minimum viable product (MVP). The simplest version of a product that lets you learn whether customers want it. It is a learning tool, not a bad product.

Ways to test cheaply
MethodHowExample
ConciergeDo it by hand for a few customersCook and deliver 20 lunches yourself
Landing pageDescribe the offer and measure sign-upsA simple page with a 'join the waiting list' button
Pre-orderTake deposits before buildingCollect 100 rupees from the first 30 customers
PrototypeA drawn or clickable mock-upPaper screens shown to users
PilotRun in one place for a short timeOne hostel block for four weeks
Worked example

A lunch pilot

A four-week pilot at one hostel.

  1. 60 students paid 450 rupees a week.
  2. 70% renewed in week three.
  3. Complaints about portion size were fixed in week two.

Answer. A small, real test taught more than months of planning.

Decide before you start

  • What will we learn?
  • What numbers show success or failure?
  • How long and how much will it cost?
  • What will we do with each result?

Check what you just learned

1. An MVP is:
  • A perfect product
  • A logo
  • The simplest way to learn whether customers want it (correct)
  • A budget

Learning first.

Key terms: flip and sort

Validation
Testing whether customers want it
Assumption
A belief not yet proven
MVP
Minimum viable product
Pilot
A small real-world trial
Traction
Evidence of real customer demand
keyPoints: An MVP is the cheapest way to learn.
Decide the success numbers before the test.

modules.title: Business model
modules.summary: Describe how a business creates, delivers and captures value on one page.
modules.outcome: You can fill in a lean canvas, choose a revenue model and explain your unique value.
modules.intro: A business model is a simple answer to: who is the customer, what do we give them, how do we reach them and how do we make money. Writing it down on one page forces clarity.

topics.title: The lean canvas
topics.html:
Nine boxes
BoxQuestion
Customer segmentsWho exactly is it for?
ProblemWhat are the top three problems?
SolutionWhat are the key features?
Unique value propositionWhy are we different and worth attention?
ChannelsHow will we reach customers?
Revenue streamsHow do we earn?
Cost structureWhat are the main costs?
Key metricsWhich numbers show we are on track?
Unfair advantageWhat cannot be easily copied?

A lean canvas is a hypothesis, not a plan carved in stone. As you learn from customers you cross things out and rewrite them. Its value is that it fits on one page and exposes gaps.

Worked example

A unique value proposition

Lunch for students.

  1. Weak: Good food at a good price.
  2. Better: A tasty, healthy lunch in under five minutes, at a fixed price, with no queue.

Answer. A strong proposition names a benefit a customer can feel and a competitor would struggle to claim.

Tip

Fill it in with pencil. Mark the boxes you are least sure about and test those first.

Check what you just learned

1. A lean canvas is best viewed as:
  • Fixed truth
  • A pitch deck
  • A tax form
  • A set of hypotheses to test (correct)

Learn and revise.
keyPoints: A lean canvas describes the business on one page and is a hypothesis.
A strong value proposition is specific and hard to copy.

topics.title: Revenue models
topics.html:
Common ways to earn
ModelHow it worksExample
Product saleSell unitsA shop selling notebooks
SubscriptionRecurring payment for continuing accessA weekly lunch plan, a gym
CommissionA share of transactionsA marketplace taking 10%
AdvertisingOthers pay to reach your audienceA free app with sponsors
FreemiumFree basic, paid upgradeA learning app
Service feeCharge for time or workTutoring, repairs

Choosing a model

  • What are customers used to paying for?
  • Is the value delivered once or repeatedly?
  • How much does it cost you to serve each customer?
  • Can you charge before the cost, to protect cash?

Common mistakes

  • Giving everything free and planning to 'monetise later' without a path.
  • Underpricing because you fear rejection.
  • Copying a competitor's price without checking your costs.

Check what you just learned

1. A subscription suits value that is:
  • Delivered repeatedly (correct)
  • Delivered once
  • Never delivered
  • Free

Recurring value, recurring payment.
keyPoints: Pick a revenue model that matches how customers value what you give.
Do not underprice or leave money to 'later'.

topics.title: Pricing
topics.html:
Three approaches
ApproachIdeaCaution
Cost-plusCost plus a marginIgnores what customers value
Competitor-basedNear what rivals chargeTheir costs may differ from yours
Value-basedBased on the benefit to the customerNeeds good customer understanding
Formula · Price check

price must exceed the variable cost of a unit, and units sold must cover fixed costs

At 100 rupees a meal with 60 variable cost, each meal earns 40 towards fixed costs.

Practical tips

  • Test prices with real customers; ask for pre-orders at different prices.
  • Offer simple choices: two or three options.
  • Do not compete on being the cheapest unless you really have the lowest costs.
  • Raise prices when demand outstrips supply and quality is high.
Watch out

Be honest about prices and terms. Hidden charges and misleading discounts damage trust and may break consumer laws.

Check what you just learned

1. Pricing only on cost ignores:
  • Cost
  • Customer value (correct)
  • Arithmetic
  • Margin

Value matters too.

Key terms: flip and sort

Business model
How a venture creates and captures value
Value proposition
The benefit promised to the customer
Revenue stream
A source of income
Subscription
Recurring payment
Commission
A share of transactions
keyPoints: Price from value, check costs and test with real customers.
Be honest about prices.

modules.title: Money and unit economics
modules.summary: Understand costs, break-even, cash flow and whether each sale is profitable.
modules.outcome: You can calculate contribution, margin and break-even, build a six-month cash plan and explain the difference between profit and cash.
modules.intro: Many businesses fail while 'profitable' on paper because they run out of cash. Understanding a few simple numbers keeps you alive and gives you credibility with partners and lenders.

topics.title: Costs, contribution and break-even
topics.html:
Two kinds of cost
TypeMeaningExamples
FixedDoes not change with volume in the short runRent, salaries, subscriptions
VariableChanges with each unit soldIngredients, packaging, delivery
Formula · Contribution per unit

contribution = price − variable cost per unit

100 − 60 = 40 rupees per meal.

Formula · Break-even volume

break-even units = fixed costs / contribution per unit

36,000 / 40 = 900 meals a month.

Break-even explorer

Change price, cost and fixed costs and see where the business breaks even.

Adjust Price per unit (rupees), Variable cost per unit, Fixed costs per month, Units sold per month and see Contribution per unit, Break-even units (rounded down), Monthly profit change.

Watch out

If price is less than variable cost, selling more makes losses bigger. Fix price or cost before trying to grow.

Check what you just learned

1. Price 100, variable cost 60, fixed cost 36,000. Break-even units?
  • 360
  • 1,200
  • 900 (correct)
  • 600

36,000 / 40 = 900.
keyPoints: Contribution = price − variable cost.
Break-even = fixed costs / contribution.

topics.title: Profit is not cash
topics.html:
Profit is revenue minus costs over a period. Cash is the money actually in the bank. They differ because of timing: you may pay suppliers before customers pay you, buy equipment that is spread over years in the accounts, or pay a deposit in advance.

Example: six months
MonthRevenueCostsProfitCash at end
18,00030,000-22,00028,000
215,00031,000-16,00012,000
324,00032,000-8,0004,000
433,00033,00004,000
542,00034,0008,00012,000
650,00035,00015,00027,000

With 50,000 in starting cash, the business reaches its lowest balance of 4,000 in months 3 and 4. A slightly slower start would have meant running out. This low point tells you how much money you need.

Cash habits

  • Forecast cash month by month.
  • Know your lowest point and keep a buffer.
  • Invoice promptly and follow up on payments.
  • Take deposits or payment in advance when possible.
  • Separate business and personal money.

Check what you just learned

1. Why can a profitable business run out of cash?
  • It cannot
  • Luck
  • Tax only
  • Timing of payments and spending (correct)

Cash timing matters.
keyPoints: Profit and cash differ by timing.
Forecast cash and find the lowest balance.

topics.title: Startup costs and record keeping
topics.html:
One-off versus ongoing
TypeExamples
One-off start-up costsEquipment, registration and licences, first stock, website set-up
Ongoing costsRent, wages, utilities, marketing, software

Simple bookkeeping

  1. Record every sale and expense on the day.
  2. Keep receipts and invoices.
  3. Reconcile with the bank statement each month.
  4. Review a simple profit and loss summary monthly.
  5. Set aside money for taxes.
Watch out

Registration, licences, tax and labour rules differ by country and by type of business. Check the rules where you operate or get advice from a qualified accountant or adviser before you start trading.

Tip

A simple spreadsheet kept up to date beats an advanced system you never open.

Check what you just learned

1. Good record keeping means:
  • Recording on the day (correct)
  • Doing it yearly
  • Guessing
  • Skipping receipts

Small, frequent habits.

Key terms: flip and sort

Fixed cost
A cost that does not change with volume
Variable cost
A cost per unit
Contribution
Price minus variable cost
Break-even
Volume where profit is zero
Cash flow
Money moving in and out
keyPoints: Separate one-off from ongoing costs.
Keep simple, regular records and check legal and tax rules.

questions.explanation: It is the amount each unit adds towards fixed costs.
How many to cover fixed costs.
Pay and receive at different times.

options: Vary by country and business type

modules.title: Marketing and selling
modules.summary: Win your first customers, measure what each costs and keep them.
modules.outcome: You can choose channels for a small budget, calculate CAC and LTV and run a simple sales conversation.
modules.intro: A great product that nobody knows about will not survive. Early on, the best marketing is direct: talk to people, ask for the sale and learn what works.

topics.title: Finding your first customers
topics.html:
Do things that do not scale

  1. Personally invite your first 10 to 50 customers.
  2. Go where they already are: hostels, groups, local markets.
  3. Ask each customer how they found you and who else needs this.
  4. Do the work by hand; the learning is the product.
  5. Collect testimonials and photos with permission.
Early channels
ChannelCostBest for
Direct conversationsTimeLearning and first sales
Word of mouth and referralsLowTrusted, local services
Messaging groupsLowCommunities
Social media contentTimeBuilding awareness
PartnershipsTimeReaching an existing audience
Paid adsMoneyScaling what already works
Tip

Do not pay for advertising until you know a customer is worth more than they cost to win.

Check what you just learned

1. Early on you should:
  • Wait for customers to find you
  • Talk to customers personally (correct)
  • Spend all on ads
  • Hide the product

Direct contact teaches.
keyPoints: Win the first customers personally and learn from them.
Advertise only after unit economics work.

topics.title: CAC, LTV and retention
topics.html:
Formula · Customer acquisition cost

CAC = marketing and sales spend / new customers won

12,000 / 60 = 200 rupees per customer.

Formula · Lifetime value

LTV = profit per period × number of periods a customer stays

450 × 40% × 8 weeks = 1,440 rupees.

Formula · The ratio

LTV / CAC

1,440 / 200 = 7.2. A ratio of 3 or more is often seen as healthy; below 1 means losing money on each customer.

Is a customer worth winning?

Change the inputs to see CAC, LTV and the ratio.

Adjust Marketing spend (rupees), New customers, Weekly price (rupees), Margin (percent), Weeks a customer stays and see CAC, LTV, LTV to CAC ratio change.

Retention is the cheapest growth. Keeping customers longer raises LTV without extra acquisition cost. Ask customers why they leave and fix the top reason.

Check what you just learned

1. LTV to CAC below 1 means:
  • Great
  • Break-even
  • Losing money on each customer (correct)
  • Impossible

Each customer costs more than they return.
keyPoints: CAC is cost to win; LTV is profit over the relationship.
LTV/CAC should be well above 1; retention raises LTV.

topics.title: Selling honestly
topics.html:
Handling objections
ObjectionResponse
It is too expensiveCompare with the cost of the problem or offer a smaller package
I need to thinkAsk what would help them decide
I already use somethingAsk what they like and dislike about it
I do not trust new businessesOffer a trial, guarantee or references
Watch out

Never overpromise, hide costs or pressure people. Trust is a start-up's most valuable asset, and consumer protection laws exist in most places.

Tip

Asking for the sale is a skill. Practise saying: 'Would you like to start with the weekly plan today?'

Check what you just learned

1. When a customer says 'It is too expensive', you can:
  • Argue
  • Lie about price
  • Hang up
  • Compare with the cost of the problem or offer a smaller option (correct)

Show value or flexibility.

Key terms: flip and sort

CAC
Customer acquisition cost
LTV
Customer lifetime value
Retention
Keeping customers
Referral
A customer recommending you
Objection
A customer's reason for hesitating
keyPoints: Listen, match, handle doubts honestly, ask, follow up.
Never overpromise.

modules.title: Funding, legal basics and pitching
modules.summary: Choose a funding route, understand legal basics and pitch clearly.
modules.outcome: You can compare funding sources, name key legal choices to check and deliver a one-minute pitch.
modules.intro: Not every business needs outside money, and not all money is equal. Knowing your options helps you stay in control, and a clear pitch helps you win support from customers, partners and investors.

topics.title: Funding options
topics.html:
Sources of money
SourceProsCons
Bootstrapping (savings and revenue)Full control, disciplineSlower growth
Friends and familyQuick, flexibleCan strain relationships; agree terms in writing
Grants and competitionsNo repayment, no share givenCompetitive; rules and reporting
Bank or micro loansKeep ownershipMust repay with interest, even if sales fall
Angel and venture investorsLarge sums, mentoringYou give up a share; they expect high growth
CrowdfundingTests demand and raises moneyNeeds a strong campaign; commitments to backers

Investors buy a share of the business. That means you share future profit and some decisions. This suits fast-growing ventures with big markets, but not a neighbourhood shop.

Questions to ask before taking money

  1. How much do I need and what for?
  2. What will I give up: control, share, flexibility?
  3. What happens if things go badly?
  4. Can I reach profit without it?
Watch out

Be careful with unregulated lenders, schemes promising guaranteed returns, and any request for upfront fees. Check licences and read agreements, and take independent advice before signing.

Check what you just learned

1. Equity investors typically expect:
  • Fast growth and a share of the business (correct)
  • Free money
  • Nothing
  • A fixed small interest

They own a part.
keyPoints: Match funding to the business: bootstrap, loan, grant or equity.
Know what you give up.

topics.title: Legal and team basics
topics.html:
Rules differ widely by country, so this is a checklist of things to find out, not legal advice.

Things to check
AreaQuestion
Business structureSole proprietor, partnership, company? What are the liability and tax differences?
Registration and licencesWhat permits do I need (for food, for example)?
TaxWhich taxes apply, and when do I file?
ContractsAre agreements with customers, suppliers and co-founders in writing?
Intellectual propertyDo I own my name, logo and content? Am I using others' work legally?
Data and privacyAm I protecting customers' personal data?
EmploymentWhat rules apply to hiring and paying people?

Working with co-founders

  • Agree roles, time and money in writing.
  • Agree what happens if someone leaves.
  • Discuss how decisions are made.
  • Be honest about expectations early.
Tip

A one-hour talk with a qualified adviser early can save months of trouble later.

Check what you just learned

1. Agreements with co-founders should be:
  • Verbal only
  • In writing (correct)
  • Secret
  • Avoided

Clarity prevents disputes.
keyPoints: Check structure, licences, tax, contracts, IP and data rules.
Put agreements with co-founders in writing.

topics.title: The pitch
topics.html:
A longer deck
SlideContent
ProblemWho suffers and how much
SolutionWhat you do
MarketHow big and how reachable
TractionPilots, sales, partners
Business modelPrice and unit economics
TeamWhy you can do it
AskHow much and what for

Pitch tips

  • Start strong and speak slowly.
  • Use numbers and a short story.
  • Show you understand the customer.
  • Be honest about risks.
  • Practise aloud with a timer.
  • End by repeating the ask.

Common mistakes

  • Starting with the company history.
  • Claiming 'no competition'.
  • Unrealistic projections.
  • Reading from slides.

Check what you just learned

1. A pitch should end with:
  • A joke
  • A long history
  • A clear ask (correct)
  • An apology

Say what you want.

Key terms: flip and sort

Bootstrapping
Funding with your own money and revenue
Equity
A share of ownership
Grant
Money that need not be repaid
Pitch
A short presentation to win support
Traction
Evidence of customer demand
keyPoints: Problem, solution, traction, model, ask.
Use numbers, be honest, practise aloud.
